draft.title: Services across borders
card: A service is work done for a customer, such as answering a question, fixing a bill or giving advice. It is not a physical product.
Fast internet and phone links let a business provide a service from far away. The worker and the customer can be in different countries.
Many Australian companies use call centres in India and the Philippines to answer customer calls and chats. Staff there may work through the night to match Australian daytime hours.
A business may choose a distant country for reasons such as lower wage costs or a large pool of skilled, English-speaking workers. This links the places and people involved in one service.
draft.remember: Fast internet lets a service be done in one country for a customer in another.

a.q: What makes it possible for a call centre in the Philippines to serve a customer in Australia?
opts: Fast internet and phone links that join the two places
A road and rail network that joins the two countries
A shipping route that carries the service by sea
Both places sharing the same time zone and climate
a.why: A service is not a physical product, so it can travel through internet and phone links. Shipping is tempting, but it moves goods, not services like answering a call.
a.clue: A service is not a physical thing that needs to be carried.

b.q: Tom in Perth chats online with a bank worker in Manila about his account. Which of these best describes what is happening?
opts: A service is provided across borders by fast internet
A product is moved along a supply chain by ship
Internet access is being kept from a remote area
A worker is travelling overseas to meet a customer
b.why: The bank worker helps Tom from another country using the internet, so a service crosses borders. It is not a product moving by ship, because nothing physical is sent.
b.clue: Ask whether anything physical is moving, or only the work.

a.best: Fast internet and phone links that join the two places

b.best: A service is provided across borders by fast internet

problems.detail: The card says staff in India and the Philippines may work through the night to match Australian daytime hours. That fits India, which is 4.5 to 5.5 hours behind eastern Australia. The Philippines is only 2 to 3 hours behind eastern Australia and in the same time zone as Perth, so night shifts are not needed there. Students could get a false idea of the time difference.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer and the explanations match the card. One card line suggests Philippine staff work through the night to match Australian hours, but the Philippines is only 2 to 3 hours behind eastern Australia and shares Perth's time zone, so the line should refer only to India or be reworded.
